PREFACE 


HE PREFACE to the first edition of “Who’s Who in Engineer- 

ing” published in 1922, stated that it was the “intention of the 

publishers to make biennial revision ..., the second edition .. 
to appear, with substantial additions, in May, 1924.” Since that time 
the work has come under publishing auspices that have given it com- 
piling and publication facilities commensurate with its own importance, 
and has become part of a large and long established organization 
devoted to the production of high grade publications. This change 
of ownership interrupted the original plans for its appearancé, and 
thus the second edition, though placed upon a regular biennial schedule 
of revision, appears-one year later than was the plan when the first 
edition came from the press. 


There are several points, believed by the publishers to be of ex- 
cellence, that it is desired to call to the attention of the public. First, 
that this edition contains between 18,000 and 19,000 brief biographies 
of individuals with claim to representation in a volume dealing with 
the engineering profession. It is international in scope and future 
editions will attempt to give even more space to the engineering frat- 
ernity of other continents. The achievements herein recounted in 
abbreviated fact are those ‘which form the absorbingly interesting and 
almost unbelievably impressive history of modern engineering. Second, 
we offer the high standard of qualification that we have attempted to 
hold as a guide. Objection might be made ‘as to laxity or strictness 
in this particular, but a conscientious effort has been consistently put 
forth to make this a work thoroughly representative of the best in 
engineering. In those cases where names sought are not found the 
explanation of the omission is probably. that the requested data were not 
supplied by the individuals. We have asked and now seek the coopera- 
tron of the profession toward the inclusion of any outstanding engineers 
whose names are missing from the following pages. Third, the geo- 
graphical index, which has greater potential value than almost any other 
single feature of the book. Fourth, the fact that as one of a series of 
established and highly regarded “Who’s Who” publications, ‘““Who’s 
Who in Engineering” has a permanence and substantiality that are 
assurance of quality and meticulous care in the future. 


Paid material is not accepted for this volume. 


We would be remiss in courtesy and duty if we failed to recognize 
the cordial helpfulness and cooperation of the engineering societies 
and the industrial organizations whose staffs play an important part 
in the present volume. 

THE PUBLISHERS

of. Engrs, W.aS: oe served as asst on railroad

and detachment at taking of Ft. Fisher; 7 brevets, 
the highest that of Major General. At Ft. Totten 
made expts with high explosives; devised adopted 
system of Coast Defence by submarine mines; 
established Engr School of Application; served on 
many Engr Bds of Army, including Bd of Ord- 
nance and Fortification, and Engr Bd for our 
Coast Defences (pres.).. On special commissions 
made three trips to. Europe: to Italy, 1870, to 
observe solar eclipse; in 1875 to contract for 
submarine mining cable; in 1888 on Joint Army

cannon. After retirement, chmn Jury of Higher 
Awards, Atlanta Expn; made extended ener gee

Nat. Acad. Sciences; in 1891 became mem. Mates 
nal Comité Technique of the New French Panama 
Canal Co., and its consulting engr until. the prop- 
erty passed to United States in 1904, residing in 
Paris, on the Isthmus, and in U. S., receiving and 
forwarding reports of operations to the company, 
and to Isthmian Canal Commn at Washington; 
after transfer mem Am. Bd of Consulting Engrs 
which determined plan of canal; meanwhile served 
as prof. hydraulic engr in post-graduate courses, 
George Washington Univ. Protestant Episcopal- 
ian. Mem. Am. Philos. Soc., Nat. Acad. Sciences, 
Am. Acad, Arts and Sciences, New Orleans Acad, 
Sciences; corr. mem. Imperial Royal »Geol. Soc. 
of Austria. Hereditary mem. (representing Capt. 
Nathan Hale) of Soc. of the Cincinnati (pres. 
Conn. Branch). Publs: Physics and Hydraulics

Artillery in the Campaign Against Richmond; 

periments to Develop a System of Submarine 
Mines; Problems of the Panama Canal; Half Cen-

technical press.

ACHESON, (Dr.) Edward Goodrich, 35 West 
42nd St.; res. 180 Riverside Drive, New 
York City. 

Elec. Engr, Chemist, Inventor, Scientist; b. 


Washington, Pa., March 9, 1856; s. William Ache- 
son (iron mfr) and Sarah Diana (Ruplé) Acheson; 
g. s. David Acheson, who came from Glassdrum- 
mond, County Armagh, Ireland, in 1798, and set- 
tled in Washington, Pa. (became prominent in 
business there and three terms mem. Gen. Assem- 
bly of Pa., with descendants prominent as lawyers 
and judges, one a Congressman, etc.); ed. in 
Bellefonte (Pa.) Acad. until 1872, when was 
taken from school to fill position in father’s blast 
furnace; hon. Sc.D., University of Pittsburgh, 
1909; m. Brooklyn, N. Y., 1884, Margaret Maher. 
Soon after father’s death in 1873, became chain- 
man with a surveying party, following with varied 
occupations, devoting leisure to “mech, research 
and invention; employed, successively, as railway 
ticket clerk, engr, bookkeeper and iron miner un- 
til 1880, when went to New York; became asst 
draftsman in laboratories of Thomas A. Edison at 
Menlo Park, 1880; sent as first asst engr of Edi- 
son interests at’ Electrical Exposition, Paris, 1881, 
and after its close remained in Paris with the 
Edison Co., and later was for a time in Italy 
with the Italian company operating the Edison 
patents, returned to. Paris,.1883, to conduct ex- 
periments on his own account on the problem of 
direct conversion of heat. into electric energy; 
these experiments and illness exhausted his sav- 
ings; on return to New York sought a salaried 
position and became supt Consolidated Camp Co., 
Brooklyn, 1884-85; invented anti-induction tele- 
phone’ wire and sold it to George Westinghouse, 
1886; elec. engr with Standard Underground 
Cable Co., Pittsburgh, 1886-89. Having in leisure 
hours become interested in electrical and chemical 
research for production of abrasives superior to 
any then in use, decided to devote entire time to 
experiments, and in March, 1891, having oppor- 
tunity to use a large electric current, began a 
series of experimental tests which led to the pro- 
duction of a new and previously unknown body 
so hard. and abrasive that it would cut diamonds, 
which he named Carborundum, patented in Feb- 
ruary, 1893. Organized the Carborundum Co., 
beginning with small plant at Monongahela City, 
which’ was: soon outgrown, and in 1895 the great 
Carborundum plant at Niagara Falls, N. Y., was 
built;:which now has the largest electrical furnace 
in. the world, with annual production of more 
than 20,000,000: Ibs.. of carborundum. With the 
excessively high temperatures made available at 
the Niagara plants, Dr, Acheson had the means 
for further experiments, with the result that in 
1897 he developed a mew process for producing 
graphite far superior in purity and quality of any 
of the graphites found in their natural state; or- 
ganized in 1899 the Acheson Graphite Co., later 
reorganized into the International Graphite Co.

of Niagara Falls (production now exceeding 50,- 


000,000 Ibs. annually), used in the manufacture 
of electrodes, in the filling of dry batteries, as a 
paint pigment for metals, as a material for use 
in electrotyping, etc.; also inventor of Siloxicon 
and Egyptianized Clay; afterward made independ- 
ent discovery of a method for producing, by 
another method, a _ practically chemically pure 
graphite (guaranteed 99 per cent. pure), a soit, 
non-coalescing graphite, unequaled, which became 
known as Deflocculated Acheson Graphite, from 
initials of which the suffix ‘dag’? was coined by 
Dr. Acheson as name for the products Gredag, 
Oildag and Aquadag for the lubricants made from 
it with grease, oil or water, as the respective vehi- 
cles, resulting in a very large increase in lubricat- 
ing efficiency. These products are made in a spe- 
cial plant at Port Huron, Mich., by a special 
corporation, the Acheson ‘Oildag "Co. Awarded 
the Perkin Gold Medal, 1910; the Rumford Medal, 
1907; also has twice received the John Scott 
Medal of the Franklin Inst. His products re- 
ceived Grand Prizes at the Paris Exposition,

ALFORD, William Valorous, Garrettsville, Ohio. 

Civil Engr, Land Surveyor; b. Windham, Port- 
age County, Ohio, Oct. 7, 1858; s. Darius Manby 
and Cathaline (Brewster) Alford; 10th generation 
on mother’s side from Elder William Brewster of 
the ‘‘Mayflower,” and 11th generation on father’s 
side from William Brewster’s only daughter, Pa- 
tience; ed. in public schools and by private tutor 
and continued study while engaged in railroad 
surveys and constrn; m. Garrettsville, Ohio, Mar. 
21, 1919, Georgia Lee Robinson. First asst engr 
on division work, Nicaragua Canal Survey, 1887; 
connected with all the surveys up to and including 
final survey in 1901; dir. engr on Darien Survey. 
Sent by Govt to make exploration survey from 
Darien to Panama along Continental Divide, and 
with Mr. G. P. Phelps, transtiman, remain the 
only two white men who have covered this entire 
distance on foot. Since canal surveys chief engr 
of several Ry Cos on surveys, construction, etc., 
also Oil and Gas Co. of Texas and Kansas; built 
million dollar oil refinery in Texas and several 
large gas pumping stations in Kansas. Last impor- 
tant work, on which continues, is a railroad from 
the Pacific to navigable water on the Amazon River 
in Northern Peru. In 1917 located a railway on 
top of the Andes for Am. Vanadium Co. During 
last 80 years has had charge of many eng. proj- 
ects. Inventor of one-rail road for cheap’ develop- 
ment of South America, which will take curves 
of 100 ft. radius and grades-up to 20 per cent. 
Fellow Royal Geog. Soc. of England. Republican. 
Presbyterian. Now on 38-year visit to Shanghai, 
China (1921-24).

ANDERSON, (Col.) William Patrick, res. 64 
Cooper St., Ottawa, Ont., Canada. 

Superannuated Govt Engr; b. Levis, P. Q., Can- 
ada, Sept. 4, 1851; s. Thomas and Adelaide A. 
(Smyth) Anderson; ed Univs of Bishops’ College 
and Manitoba; m, Ottawa, Oct. 18, 1876, Dorothea 
S. Small; four- sons: Col. William B. (C.M.G., 
D.S.O.), Col. Thomas V. (D.S.O.), Hugh B. (mgr 
Bank of Nova Scotia), and Major Alexander A. 
(D.S.O.); one dau., Dorothy (wife of Major O. S. 
Tyndale K. C. Montreal). Entered the Civil Ser- 
vice of the Dominion Govt as asst engr in Oct., 
1874; promoted to chief engr. Dept. of Marine and 
Fisheries and Gen. Supt of Lighthouses of the dom- 
inion Govt, Feb., 1880. Duties included the constrn 
and repairs to Govt. steamers and construction 
and maintenance of lighthouses, lightships, fog 
alarms, buoys and beacons; supervision of constrn 


and equipment of lifeboats, the removal of wrecks 
and obstructions in navigable waters; tidal and 
current surveys; hydrographic surveys; publica- 
tion, examination and correction of. hydrographic 
charts; constrn and repair to fish hatcheries and 
refrigerators ; engineering pionts in connection with 
the construction and maintenance of fish passes; 
supervision of surveys of oyster beds; examinations 
for applications for foreshore, wharf and water lots 
as they affect the interests of navigation; prepara- 
tion and publication of notices to mariners and 
hydrographic notes. During occupancy of this 
office, designed and erected more than 500 light- 
houses and 80 fog-alarm installations, ~ building 
more lighthouses and other aids to navigation than 
any other man that ever lived or that probably 
ever will live, because his services in this field 
were during Canada’s formative period when the 
Dominion’s immense coastline was being marked 
(a similar opportunity can never recur). Special 
achievements include a complete hydroghraphic 
survey of the Bay of Quinte; constrn of a light- 
house on a caisson foundation in 13 feet of water 
on Colchester reef, and another in 14 feet. of wat- 
er in Pelee Passage, Lake Erie, fire-proof through- 
out; the building of a permanent lighthouse in the 
traverse of St. Roch in 42 feet of water and a 
tideway of over 7 knots; the installation of a 
first-order siren, worked by compressed air, on 
Belle Isle, with power obtained from the lakes on 
the hills; and the installation of an occulting elec- 
tric light and electrically operated fog alarm on 
a shoal in Victoria Harbor, B. Edited Wal- 
bran’s ‘‘Coast Names of British Columbia,’ a 
‘‘“Handbook of Indian Place Names in the Maritime 
Provinces,’’ and. compiled a ‘‘List of Place Names 
on Anticosti Isi:tid.’’ Treas. Dominion of Canada 
Rifle Assn.; well-known rifle-shot, having rep- 
resented Canada at Bisley, and in 1900 won. Gov- 
ernor-General’s Match; comd 48d Battalion, Ot- 
tawa and Carlton Rifles until Jan., 1892, when was 
placed on retired list. Mem. Inst. Civil Engrs of 
Great Britain (sometime mem. Council); charter 
mem, and past pres., E.I.C.; mem. Eng Standards 
Assn of Canada; chairman Geog. Bd. of Canada, 
Lighthouse Bd of Canada; trustee and executor, 
estate of late Thomas Anderson, of Edmonton, 
Alberta; sole executor of late Vic. Anderson, of 
Calgary, Alberta. Recreations: Golf, curling. 
Club: Royal Ottawa Golf. Moderate conserva- 
tive in politics. Presbyterian.

hundred supervising engrs and organized details

tracts, aggregating many millions of dollars, in 
plants from Indiana to the Pacific and from N. 
Dak. to Texas. Since armistice senior mem.

ATTERBURY, (Brig. Gen.) William Wallace, 


Broad St. Station, Philadelphia. 

Railway Official, Civil, Mech. and Mil. Engr; 
b. New Albany, Ind., Jan. 31, 1866; s. John G. 
and Catharine J. (Larned) Atterbury; g.s. of 
Lewis Atterbury and of Catharine Boudinot, who 
was niece of Elias Boudinot, who served as pres. 
of the Continental Congress; Ph.B., 1886, hon. 
A.M., 1911, Yale Univ.; L.L.D., Univ. of Pas 
1919. Entered railway service as apprentice in 
Altoona shops of The Pennsylvania R.R., 1886-89; 
asst road foreman of engines on various divisions 
of Pennsylvania R. R. and the Philadelphia, Wil- 
mington and Baltimore R.R., 1889-92; asst engr 
of motive power in Pennsylvania Co.’s Northwest 
System, 1892-93; master’ mechanic for Pennsyl- 
vania Co. at Fort Wayne, Ind., 1893-96; supt 
motive power of Pa. Lines East of Pittsburgh and 
Erie, 1896-1901, gen. supt of motive power 1901- 
02; gen. mgr Pa. Lines East of Pittsburgh and 
Erie Jan. 1, 1903-March 24, 1909; fifth V.p. in 
charge of Transportation 1909-11, becoming 4th - 
v-p. March 3, 1911, until May 8, 1912, when prac- 
tice of designating vice-presidents numerically 
was discontinued, and he became y.p. in charge 
of operation, which position (except during his 
war service period), he has retained ever since. 
Elected, May 17, 1916, pres. of Am. Ry Assn, in 
which capacity rendered valuable service to U. S. 
Govt in connection with transportation of troops 
and supplies to the Mexican Border and the At- 
lantic Seaboard. Soon after U. S. entered war 
against Germany, was apptd Director General of 
Transportation of A.E.F., in charge of details of 
constrn and operation of U. S. transportation re- 
quirements in France, and the harmonizing of 
them with those of our Allies in France. Sailed 
for Europe in August, 1917; commd Brig.-Gen. 
U. S.-A., October 5, 1917; returned to U. S. 
May 31, 1919, and received discharge from Army 
on June 1, 1919. Received Distinguished Service 
Medal (U. S.), Legion of Honor, with rank of 
Commander (France); Companion of Most Noble 
Order of the Bath (Great Britain); and Com- 
mander of the Order of the Crown (Belgium). 
Has. taken leading parts in work of rehabilitation

BARBOUR 


a ce 


1915, Bertha Louise Alexandra Hildenbrand ; ch. : 
John Worthington, Marie Louise, Robert Cecil, 
Suzanne Alexandra. In 1908 began building and 
flying aircraft of his own design; the fourth or 
fiith Englishman to fly; designed, built and flew 
the first all-British airplane; during 1908 and 1912 
designed, built and flew 28 various types of air- 
craft and taught numerous officers and others to 
fly; presented a squadron of four aircraft to British 
Govt., 1911; in the autumn of 1912 gave up active 
flying and became aeronautical consultant for 
various interests, including principal British mfrs. 
and Lloyd’s, etc; prior to War completed official 
tests as an airship pilot; organized the works of 
the Aircraft Mfg. Co. (which later became the 
largest aircraft constructors in Eng.) ; visited 
Turkey during the Turko-Bulgarian War, and had 
charge of their military airplanes; thus probably 
the first aviator to see active service; volunteered 
in 1914 and served as an

ural and casing-head gasoline; also solvents from —

of Colonel Burrell and G. G. Oberfell. Now also 
pres. Burrell Technical Supply Co. of Pittsburgh;

CARY 


while with that company invented a test system 
for multiple switchboards and designe] and in- 
stalled the first metallic circuit multiple switch- 
board put into service; with Western Elec. Co., 
1887-89, during which service made many im- 
portant improvements in design and.. installatiou 
of telephone cables and switchboards, including a 
fundamental invention upon which present com- 
mon battery switchboard is. bascd; with Metro- 
politan Telephone and Telegraph Co. later the 
New York Telepnone Co.), 1889-1907, as. «lec- 
trician and later as chief ehgr, and during this 
period introduced many improvements into the 
telephone system. Important among these from 
an eng. standpoint were his investigations relating 
to the transposition of telephone circuits, the re- 
sults of which are now universally applied, and 
his invention of the bridging bell, which permitted 
the placing of many more stations on a line than 
theretofore possible without impairing the trans- 
Mission of speech. This latter development made 
practical the furnishing of telephone service in 
rural sections, and is now used universally on 
farmers’ lines. For these and other inventions 
the Franklyn Inst. conferred upon him the Edward 
Longstreth Medal of Merit, and he later received 
the Franklin Medal for his engineering work. He 
was made, in 1908, Chief Engr, Am. Telephone 
and Telegraph Co., in which position directed the 


‘eng. work of the entire Bell System, and under 


his direction the Transcontinental telephone line, 


3,400 miles long, and the Washington to Boston. 


underground cable system, 425 miles long, were 
put in operation; also, under his direction, wire- 
less telephone -communication was_ established 
from the Naval Radio Station at Arlington, Va, 
to the Hawaiian Islands and the Eiffel Tower at 
Paris, France. Awarded the Edison. Medal by 
A.1.E.E. for his work in the science and art of 
telephone eng. Apptd, 1919, vice-pres., Am. Tele- 
phone and Telegraph Co., in charge of the Dept 
of Development and Research of the Bell System, 


which employs a staff of more than 2,000 people 


devoted exclusively to scientific research and de- 
velopment pertaining to new signaling methods and 
devices to be employed in both telegraphy and 
telephony; one of the many scientific and eng. 


_accomplishments of the staff under his direction 


was the feat of transmiting the speeches: of Presi- 
dent Harding and others at the Arlington Ceme- 
tery on Armistice Day, 1921, to 150,000 people 
in Washington, New York, and San Francisco. 
Before outbreak of the war he was commissioned 
as Major, and later promoted to. Col., Signal 
Corps; directed organization among the em- 
ployees of the Bell System of 12 battalions of 
trained Signal Corps troops; served with A. E. F. 
in France on staff of Brig. Gen. Edgar Russel, 
Chief Signal Officer, A. E. F., July, 1918, to 
May, 1919; signal officer in charge of communica- 
tions during armistice under Am. Commn_ to 
Negotiate Peace; recd hon. fischarae,, Jaly, et 


Promoted to Brigadier General, Oct. 93, 1921. 
_Recd decorations Distinguished Service Medal 
(U. S.), Officier Légion d’Honneur (France).

COTTRELL, Frederick Gardner, Fixed Nitrogen 
Research Laboratory, Department of Agricul- 
ture, Massachusetts and Nebraska aves., Wash- 
ington, D. C. ; 

Chem. and Cons. Metallurgist; b, Oakland, Calif., 

Jan. 10, 1877; s. Henry and Cynthia L. (Durfee) 

Cottrell; family Am. on both sides—Cottrell side 

British before coming to U. S.; the Durfee 

branch, through White family, of Mayflower de- 

scent; ed. Horton (private) school (Oakland), 

Oakiand High School; Univ. of Calif., 1893-97 

(Le Conte fellow 1896-97, B.S. 1896); Univ. of 

Berlin, 1900-01; Univ. of Leipsic, 1901-02 (Ph.D. 

1902); later when prof. in Univ. of Calif. re- 

ceived hon. membership in Alpha Chi Sigma; m., 

Nevada City, Calif., Jan. 1, 1904, Jessie M. Ful- 

ton: two children, both died in infancy. Chem. 

teacher, Oakland High School, 1897-1900; instr. 


phys. chemistry 1902-06, asst prof. 1906-11, Univ. _ 


of Calif. Cons. chemist, 1911, chief phys. chemist, 
1911-14, chief chemist, 1914-15, chief metallurgist, 
1916-19; Asst Director, 1919-20, Director, 1920-21, 
1921-22 cons. metallurgist, U.S. Bureau of 
Mines; resigned as director Jan. 1, 1921, to ‘enter 
full active service as Chairman Division of Chem- 
istry and Chemical Technology, National Re- 
search Council; July 15 to Sept. 19, 1922, Con. 
Chem. U._ S. Dept. of Agriculture, since Sept. 
19, 1922, Director Fixed Nitrogen Research Lab- 
oratory, U. S. Dept. of Agriculture. Received the 
Perkin Medal Award for 1919 from the Society of 
Chemical Industry in recognition of his notable 
work in the field of electrical precipitation. This 
work is covered by thirteen patents on processes and 
apparatus for separating and collecting particles of 
one liquid suspended in another liquid, or suspend- 
ed particles from gaseous bodies, for the purifica- 
tion of gases, for abatement of smoke, fumes and 
dust and other forms of electrical precipitation, and 
described and elaborated in many published arti- 
cles. The rights in these ‘‘Cottrell Patents’’ were 
offered to the Smithsonian Institution, in order 
that the profit resulting from the patents might be 
applied to the advancement of scientific research 
and investigation, but conditioned upon the patent 
rights being given an adequate business administra- 
tion and the proceds being devoted to furthering 


New Hampshire St., ° 


COTTRELL 460 . 


scientific research. As the first condition went be. 
yond the scope of the Smithsonian Institution the 


Research Corporation was organized in 1912 and 


has since been engaged in the business of acquiring 
patents by purchase or otherwise and developing 
and administering them, the stock receiving no 
dividends but the entire net earning of the corpora- 
tion, over and above such amounts as may be re- 
served or retained as an endowment fund or work- 
ing capital as well as other moneys and property 
of the corporation, are to be contributed to the 
Smithsonian Institution, or other scientific insti- 
tutions and societies selected by the Board of Di- 
rectors to enable them to conduct technical and 
scientific investigation research and experimenta- 
tion. The Research Corporation has thus been an 
important factor in tech. and _ scientific develop- 
ment opening doors of opportunity. Has written sev- 
eral articles, among them “On the Determination 
of Boiling Points of Solutions” (Journal of Am. 
Chem. Soc.), ‘“‘The Commercial Production of 
Helium” (Chem, and Met. Engrs), “‘La Produc- 
tion Industrielle d’L’Helium’” (Chemie et Indus- 
trie); ‘‘Recent Progress in Electrical Smoke Pre- 
cipitation,’ “The Research Corporation, an Experi- 
ment in Public Administration of Patent Rights.” 
Also testimony and reports in “Joint Hearings 
Before the Committee on Patents,” Senate and 
House Reps., 66th Cong. Went to Europe, 1919, 
as mem. commn to collect tech. information, 
visiting nearly all of the European countriés. 
Represented Nat. Acad, and Am. Chem. Soc. at 
Interallied Chem. Conference in Paris, London 
and Brussels, also Internat. Research Council, 
Brussels. Mem. A.I.M. & M.E., Am. Chem. Soc., 
Am. Electrochem. Soc., A.A.A.S. Clubs: Cosmos 
(Washington), Chemists (New York), Common- 
wealth, Engineers(San Francisco), Faculty (Calif.).

COWLES, Alfred Hutchinson, Sewaren, N. J. 


Metallurgical Engr; b. Cleveland, O., Dec. 8, 
1858; s.. Edwin and Elizabeth (Hutchinson) 
Cowles; descendant in eighth generation from 


John Cowles; b. in England 1598, came to Amer- 
ica 1628, settled at Farmington, Conn,, 1640 
(father, Edwin Cowles, famous journalist, editor 
Cleveland Leader, and one_of the founders of Re- 
publican party); ed Ohio State Univ., two years; 
Cornell Univ., four years, specializing in geol. 
chemistry; active in athletic sports in coll., dis- 
tinguished in rowing, and capt. of ’varsity four- 
oared crew, 1882; Zeta Psi; m. Akron, O., Oct. 
25, 1906, Helen J. Wills. After leaving coll. be- 
came interested with father and brother, Eugene, 
in-a large deposit of copper-zinc ore at the head 
waters of the Pecos River in San Miguel Co., N. 
Mex., which became known as the ‘‘Pecos Mines.” 
In 1905-06 individually opened up the mines on a 


‘large scale, exposing about 360,000 tons of rich 


zinc, copper, gold and silver ores. The brothers 
Cowles, investigating these mines, 1882-83, found 
ordinary methads of treating the ore a failure and 
experimented in designing an elec furnace. Eu- 
gene Cowles, the elder brother, had promoted the 
Cleveland Elec Light Co. and erected the first 
elec lighting plant in Cleveland, and A. H, Cowles, 
scientifically trained, began experiments in Cleve- 
land, 1884, in pyro-elec reduction of various me- 
tallic oxides. He found that when the tempera- 
ture of the furnace was run too high, the fireclay 
of the walls became melted and white particles of 
metal appeared at unexpected places, and he thus 
discovered the process of reducing aluminum 
which resulted in the organization of the Cowles 
Elec, Smelting and Aluminum Co, Other in- 
ventors, working on the same problem of ore re- 
duction, had achieved valuable results, notably 
Charles S. Bradley, all of whose inventions and 
discoveries relating to elec furnaces and aluminum 
were purchased by the Cowles Co. After long 
litigation the priority claim of the Cowles brothers 
as the first to use elec furnaces in the production 
of aluminum, carborundum, silicon, chromium, 
ferro-silicon, silicon-copper, fused quartz, fused 
alumina, titanium alloys, crystals of ruby and 
sapphire, graphitic carbon in large quantity and 


COWLES 466 


various alloys of the rare metals with the _baser 
metals was fully proved and sustained. Under 
their processes the Messrs. Cowles made a 10 per 
cent aluminum bronze in 1885 and sold it at 55 cents 
a pound, and were the first (Aug., 1891), to ad- 
vertise to sell pure aluminum as low as 50 cents 
per pound, thus pioneering the modern and wide- 
spread use of aluminum utensils and articles by 
average households throughout the world. In 1887 
they founded the Cowles Syndicate Co of Eng. 
which later became the British Aluminum Co. AI- 
fred Hutchinson Cowles was metallurgist of the 
Cowles. Elec. Smelting and Aluminum Co. for 
nine years; reorganized it, 1894, as the Elec 
Smelting and Aluminum Co., of which he is 
pres; also formerly pres. The Pecos Copper’ Co., 
whose mining property was sold in 1918 and has 
since been developed into one of the largest zine 
copper, gold and silver deposits in Am.  Reduc- 
tion works as yet to be completed. Author 
of important papers on metallurgical subjects on 
processes for chem. and elec. reduction of metals, 
on units for use in electrolysis, etc., and on various 
scientific subjects. In 1916 proved that silicon is 
an essential fertilizer and must be so classed along 
with potassium, phosphorus, calcium and nitrogen, 
finding that when a calcium silicate is applied to 
the soil, calcium bicarbonate and hydrate silica 
pass into solution in the soil waters, and silicon 
becomes available to plant nutrition (when, as for- 
merly tried, an alkali silicate is employed, the silicic 
acid becomes bound with lime and the alkali in 
insoluble form. Mem. A.I.E.E., A:I.M.E. (past 
pres.), Am. Electrochem. Soc., Franklin Inst. 
(Elliot Cresson and John Scott Legacy medals). 
Republican,

eas Glenn Hammond, Garden City, L. I., 
*s 


b. Hammondsport, N. Y., May 21, 
1878; s. Frank R. and Lua (Andrews) Curtiss ; 
ed. pub. schs, Hammondsport; m. Hammondsport, 
1898, Lena P. Neff. Early began expts. with mo- 
tor vehicles, establishing motorcycle factory at 
Hammondsport, 1902. Set speed records for mo- 
torcycle, riding his own machines, 1905; at Or- 
mond Beach, Fla., 1907, made record ‘for mile 
of 46-2/5 sec. with 110 ib. motorcycle. Designed 
aeronautical motors for dirigibles of Capt. T. S. 
Baldwin, 1907-09, by including motor for first 
dirigible accepted by U. S. Govt; dir. of expts 
for Aerial Expt Assn, 1907-09, and supervised 
constrn, of and piloted “June Bug,” July 4, 1908, 
for first pub. flight of mile in U. S. winning Sci- 
entific Am. trophy; experimented with the ‘‘Loon,”’ 
an aeroplane fitted with pontoons, 1908; won Gor- 
don Bennett cup and prix de la Vitesse at Rheims, 
France, Internat. Aviation Meet, as rep. Aero 
Club Am., Aug., 1909, with aeroplane and motor 
of Curtiss design; won N. Y. World prize of 
$10,000 in flight from Albany to N. Y., in 

hrs, 51 min., May 29, 1910; made pub. dem- 
onstration of hydroaeroplane, Jan., 1911, with 
which has been experimenting for number of yrs, 
following demonstration of this invention with 
that of flying boat (awarded prize by Aero Club. 
Am., 1912). Awarded Collier Trophy, 1911, for 
development of hydroaeroplane; again in 1912 for 
invention of flying boat; 1913, presented the Lang- 
ley Medal by Smithsonian Inst., Wash., D. C. 
Est. flying schs at Hammondsport, San Diego, 
Buffalo, Newport News, Miami, Atlantic City, 
1909-19; introduced flying boat to Brazil, Russia, 
Austria, Italy and Germany, 1913-14; designed and 
built for Rodman Wanamaker, the “America,” the 
first multi-motored flying boat, the first heavier- 
than-air flying craft designed for transatlantic

b. Petrograd, i

Alexander and Nadine (Rabou-

towskaja) de Bothezat; de Bothezat family, one 
of most prominent noble families of BDessarabien, 
founded the town Kichinew, capital of Bessara- 
bien, in which there is a street and a square 
each named ‘‘de Bothezat’; ed. Technol. Inst. 
of Kharkow, Russia, 1902-05; Electrotech. Inst. 
Montefiore, Liege (Belgium) 1905-07, E.E. with 
Distinction, 1907; returned to Kharkow 1908, 
grad. technological engr with distinction; post- 
grad., Univs. of Gé6ttingen and Berlin, 1908-09, 
and Univ. of Paris, 1910-11; Sc.D. (with “highly 
honorable’? mention), 1911 (dissertation on ‘‘Air- 
plane Stability,” first mathematical investigation 
of that problem). Junior prof. Poly. Inst. of 
Petrograd, and head of Aeronautical Laboratory, 
also lecturer, Officer Aviation Coll., Petrograd, 
1912; scientific expert, War Dept, Petrograd, 
1913; extraordinary prof. 1914, ordinary proi. 
1915, Poly. Inst.; chief constr and designer, 
aviation dept, factory Duflon & Co., 1914; mem. 
Eng. Advisory Com., Aeronautical Advisory Com. 
and Bomb-Dropping Com., Petrograd, 1915; chief 
builder of Aeronautical Inst., Odessa, and cons. 
engr of Factory lgora, 1916; pres., Aviation 
Testing Field Cou and pres., Scientific Com., 
Russian Aero Club, 1917; came to U. S. May, 
1918; lectured at Mass. Inst. Tech. and Columbia 
Univ., June, 1918; Univ. of Chicago, Dec., 1919; 
Univ. of Michigan, May, 1924; from July, 1918 
to June, 1921, scientific expert, Nat. Advisory 
Com. for Aeronautics, Washington, D. C. Author 
of various reports, lectures and contributions on 
the dynamics of aeronautics; aerial ballistical 
tables; an introduction into the Study of the 
Laws ot Air Resistance of Aerofoils; General 
Theory of Blade-Screws (Fourth Ann. Report of 
Nat. Advisory Com. for Aeronautics), 1919; 
General Theory of the Airplane Steady Motion 
(Sixth Ann. Report of N.A.C.A.), 1920; The 
Meaning for Humanity of the Aerial Crossing of 
the Ocean (Scientific Monthly), Nov., 1919. Pro- 
posed, 1910, the use of the negative lift tails for 
securing stability (now used on nearly all air- 
planes); established, 1911, the existence, of the 
long period oscillation of the airplane, and in- 
vented the first aerofoil suspension, which gives 
complete stability of any aerofoil without tail 
plane, and other apparatus for stabilization. As 
chief constructor and designer of the factory of 
Duflon & Co. from 1914 invented gyroscopical 
sighting apparatus; sighting apparatus with in- 
terior hydrodynamical damping, maintaining the 
vertical; mechanical apparatus for propeller se- 
lection; designed and built various types of air- 
planes, fans (big mining fans), windmills, air 
and marine propellers; new hydroplane type for 
the high seas; introduced the use of plane radial 
screws. From June, 1921 to May, 1923, Acting 
Chief of the Special Research Section, Eng. Div., 
Mcvook Field, Dayton, Ohio. Inventor, designer 
and builder of the ‘‘de Bothezat Helicopter’, the 
first Helicopter in the History of Aeronautics to 
actually perform sustained men carrying flights. 
This Helicopter was built and tested at McCook 
Field, Dayton, Ohio. From Dec., 1922 to April, 
1923, the de Bothezat Helicopter flown by Col. 
T. H. Bane, chief of the Eng. Div., has made 
over one hundred flights carrying one, two and 
three passengers, the maximum total weight lifted 
being 4,400 Ibs. (with an engine delivering about 
160 h.p.). ‘This Helicopter is the first to have 
actuaily demonstrated inherent stability, complete 
controllability, and ability to hover and to descent 
motor stopped. we

DeFOREST, Lee, 1891. Sedgwick Av., Bronx; 


res. 232nd St. and Riverside Drive, Spuyten 
Duyvil, New York. 

Radio Engr and Inventor; b. Council Bluffs, 
Iowa, Aug. 26, 1873; s. Henry Swift and Anna 
M. (Robbins) de Forest; John Alden desc. on 
mother’s side; 8th generation from French 
Huguenot settlers in Harlem (New York) on 
father’s side; prepared for coll. at Mt. Hermon 
(Mass.) Boys’ School; Ph.B. (Sheffield Sci. 
Sch.) 1896, Ph.D. 1899, Yale; D.Sc., 1919, Syra- 
cuse Univ.; m. New Jersey, Dec., 1912, ary 
Mayo, three daus, Harriot (b. 1909), Eleanor 
(b. 1919), Marilyn (b. 1924). After leaving coll. 
was for a time engaged in research work with the 
Western Elec. Co.’s telephone dept, but from 1900 
began research and business for himself. In that 
year he began developing novel types of detectors 
for wireless telegraph receiving, followed by de- 
velopment of alternating current transmitters for 
same as. distinguished from the British practice. 
Founded, 1902, the Am. DeForest Wireless Tele- 
graph Co. In 1906 perfected the audion, which 
is the most sensitive radio detector, and patented 
it in 1907. While primarily invented to improve 
radio communication, it was found, after much 
experiment, to be equally applicable to telephone 
currents, and in 1912 he brought his invention 
to the attention of the Am. Telephone & Tele- 
graph Co. with the result that its use made pos- 
sible transcontinental telephone service in’ 1915. 
By use of large oscillating audions, wireless tele- 
phony from Washington to Honolulu has been 
achieved, and.this detector has become standard 
for long distance signalling all over world, es- 
pecially in U. S. Navy service. Audion am- 
plifier consists of a small incandescent lamp bulb, 
exhausted of air, containing, in addition to the 
usual filament, two thin plates of nickel, about 
one-eighth of an inch from the filament on either 
side, between the filament and the plates are two 
pieces of nickel wire, bent grid-shaped. Has taken 
out over 100 patents on wireless signalling; most 
important being the audion, horizontal receiving 
antenae and duplex sending and receiving devices. 
Has contributed occasional papers for elec. publi- 
cations and Inst. of Radio Engrs. In 1913 or- 
ganized DeForest Radio Telephone & Telegraph 
Co., of which is pres. Was mem. of original 
Yale Battery of Field Arty in Spanish-Am. War, 
1898. Awarded’ gold medal at St. Louis: Uni- 
versal Exp., 1904, and by Panama-Pacific In- 
ternat. Expn, San Francisco, 1915, for the part 
his audion amplifier played in transcontinental 
telephone service opening that year, as well as 
for the oscillon and audion detector which made 
possible transoceanic radio telephone communica- 
tion from Arlington to Honolulu and Paris, Nov., 
1915. The Audion has revolutionized all Radio, 
“wired wireless,” and long-distance telephony 
throughout the world. Since 1921 invented and 
perfected the ‘‘Phonofilm” or talking motion_pic- 
tures by photography of sound waves. Elliot 
Cresson medal; Cross of Legion of Honor; Prix 
Saint Tour Inst. de France. Fellow A.I.E.E., Inst. 
Radio Engrs (pres., 1909-10), Franklin Inst., 
N. Y. Elec. Soc.; trustee, Am. Defense Soc. 
Recreation: Motoring. Club: Yale (New York). 
Progressive Republican, Agnostic.

New York, milena 

Mech, Engr; b. New York, N. Y., June 20, 
1872; s. William Noble and Mary Elizabeth (Cole- 
man) Dickinson; maternal ancestor settled in Nan- 
tucket in 1630; on father’s side came from En- 
gland two generations back, but others of that 
line, including related Montagues and Bradleys, 
settled in New England at an earlier date; ed in 
Brooklyn Collegiate and Polytechnic Inst, by pri- 
vate tutor and trade school shop practice. With 
Elektron Mfg Co., Brooklyn, N. Y., and Spring- 
fieid, Mass., personal work on bench, foreman of 
winding room and of testing room, supt of con- 
strn, mgr of Boston office, and vice-pres.; estab- 
lished and was propr of W. Noble Dickinson, Jr., 
& Co., in New York, until on invitation became 
connected with the Otis Elevator Co., first in 
temporary charge of the Chicago works and Mid- 
dle West constrn, later in charge of engineering on 
Pacific Coast; alternating current machine devel- 
opment and investigation abroad; became mgr 
foreign dept and 2nd v.-p. of Otis Elevator Co. of 
Maine (subsidiary for transacting business in for- 
eign countries). Later organized the General 
Elevator Co. (29 Broadway, New York), as propr 
and chief engr, and the good-will of that com- 
pany was acquired by the Standard Plunger Ele- 
vator Co., of which was pres., gen. mgr, and one 
of the five directors. These positions he resigned 
upon urgent call from the Chief of Ordnance U.S. 
Army to go to Washington early in 1918 to serve 
during the World War. During war period was 
mem. Home Defense League and head of Artillery 
Branch No. 1 (which was concerned with the T5- 
millimetre field gun program and the ant-aircraft 
guns), Progress Section, Ordnance Dept, U. S. 
Army. Following the armistice was requested to 
place the history of this work in form for perma- 
nent record. This was followed by similar re- 
quests with relation to trench warfare, material, 
military pyrotechnics, drop bombs and release 
mechanisms and sights (the latter covering the 
Ordnance Dept activities in connection with bomb- 
ing from the air). Author of several U. S. Army 
ordnance publications. Has presented tech. papers 
before New York Elec Soc. and Nat. Elec Light 
Assn, and discourses on South American condi- 
tions before N. Y. Chapter of Am. Inst. of 
Banking. Mem. .A.S.M.E:; ° fellow. A.I.E.E.: 
Past Pres. N. Y. E. S. former mem. U. S.. Revol- 


_vor Assn, Recreations: Horseback riding, tennis, 
suiling. Club: Engineers (New York). Republi- 
ean. | Episcopalian.

and Traction Co.: engr and mgr, and later pres., 
Denver Gas and Electric Co. In 1905 organized 
firm of Henry L. Doherty & Co., bankers, and has 
ever since conducted it with success as a medium 
for the financing of public utility operations and 
organizations. In connection there were organized 
the Doherty Operating Co. and Doherty Securi- 
ties Co., having to do with administrative features 
of the various companies and the careful market- 


ing of their securities, and later organized upon 
modern lines the Cities Service Co. for purpose of 
producing higher efficiency and undertaking the 
creation of new enterprises in the line of public 
utilities for towns having no such enterprises or 
an insufficient supply of them. Through these 
organizations many towns and cities all over the 
United States have acquired excellently function- 
ing gas, electric and traction facilities, solidly 
backed and efficiently managed from the tech. side, 
each plant being sensibly and economically man- 
aged by the local board. Mr. Doherty’s long ex- 
perience has enabled him to build up a group of 
more than fifty gas, electric light and traction 
companies in which he is pres. or dir, and give 
them the benefit of thoroughly trained men in all 
depts of eng, administrative or financial direction. 
Has made many important inventions in connec- 
tion with improved devices and methods for the 
production, purification and distribution of gas, 
meters and other gas appliances. Awarded the 
first Beall gold medal, 1898, for paper on “Gas 
for Fuel’; mem. of Organization Bd of World’s 
Congress of Electricity, St. Louis, 1904; pres., 
Ohio Gas Light Assn, 1902; Northwestern Elec- 
tric Assn, 1899; N. E. L. A., 1901; v.-p. Am. Gas 
Inst.,.. 1908. Mem. .A.I.E.E.,,.A.S.H.. & V.E.,

EDISON, Thomas Alva, West 
Llewellyn Park, Orange, N. J. 
Elec. Engr, Scientist, Inventor; b. Milan, Erie 
Co., Ohio, Feb, 11, 1847; s. Samuel and Nancy 
(Elliott) Edison; paternal descent Dutch, ma- 
ternal Scotch; family moved to Port Huron, 
Mich., 1854; early edn. chiefly from mother’s teach- 
ing; hon. Ph.D., Union Coll., 1878; D.Sc., Prince- 
ton Univ., 1915; LL.D., Univ. of State of N. Y., 
1916; m. Ist, 18738, Mary G.. Stillwell; 2nd, 1886, 
Mina Miller. Newsboy on Grand Trunk Ry 
trains between Port Huron and Detroit, 
62. (in 1862 printed and published a newspaper, 
“The Weekly Herald,” the first newspaper ever 
printed on a moving train); studied telegraphy 
under J. U. Mackenzie, station agent at Mt 
Clemens, Mich., 1862; did some work in local 
office at Port Huron, and in 1863 entered on first 
regular position as telegraph operator on Grand 
Trunk Ry, at Stratford Junction, Ont., and similar- 
ly employed in various Mid-West cities, 1863-68, 
and incidentally studied and experimented upon 
impvt of telegraphic apparatus; entered employ 
of Western Union at Boston, 1868, but soon re- 
signed to devote, entire time to experiment on du- 
plex system of telegraphy, and made first patented 
invention, Elec. Vote Recorder; with means al- 
most exhausted went from Boston to New York, 
1869, went to operating room of Gold and Stock 
Telegraph Co., seeking work, found the appa- 
ratus had broken down, nobody there able to 
fix it, offered to, and did put the plant in working 
order, and was made supt at $300 a month, 1869; 
partner with Franklin L. Pope as elec. engr, 1869- 
-(0; improved stock ticker and invented Universal 
stock ticker and “Unison” device; opened mig 
shop in Newark, N. J., mfg tickers, etc., 1870; 
assisted Sholes, inventor of the typewriter, to 
make a successful. working model, 1871; contin- 
uously engaged in inventions, completing the. Mo- 
tograph, automatic telegraph systems, duplex, quad- 
ruplex, sextuplex and multiplex telegraph appara- 
tus; paraffin paper, carbon rheostat; 
meter and carbon telephone transmitter 1871-77; 
removed from Newark to new lab. at Menlo Park, 
N. J., 1876; invented the phonograph, 1877; the 
incandescent electric lamp, 1879; new types of 
dynamo-electric machines, and improved systems 
of commercial distribution of current. for light. 
power and heat, 1879-80; invented magnetic ore 
separator, 1880; established first commercial incan- 
escent lamp factory at Harrison, N. J., 1881;

FERRIS, Theodore Ernest, 30 Church St; res. 
431 Riverside Drive, New York, N. Y. 

Naval Architect and Marine Engr; b. Stam- 
ford, Conn., Aug. 17, 1872; s. Nathaniel Betts 
and. Louise (Keeler) . Ferris; family of Norman 
origin, Henri di Ferriers receiving large land 
grants from William the Conqueror, whom he 
accompanied in the Conquest of England, name 
later Anglicized. to Ferris, the American line be 


FERVER 


ginning with Jeffrey Ferris, whom. came from 
ngland, settling in Connecticut, 16384; ed. in 
public schools of Stamford, Conn.; grad. Green- 
wich (Conn.) Acad. after course of technical 
training; m. Lois Davis Blake, of New Bedford, 
Mass.; children: Nathaniel James, Theodore Louis. 
Began shipbuilding at a yard on Long Island 
where he practically mastered the art of building 
wooden ships; after that at the John Roche ship- 
yard, Chester, Pa., studying there the constrn of 
steel vessels and beginning the study of drafting 
and designing, later working in Baltimore and 
afterward in large yards at Philadelphia, Chicago 
and Detroit. About 1890 became associated with 
the late. A. Cary Smith, distinguished marine 
painter and naval architect, with whom designed 
many river and sound steamships, yachts and 
pleasure craft until 1898; supt and constrn chief,, 
Townsend & Downey Company, Shooter’s Island, 
N. Y., 1898-1903; partner with A. Cary Smith, 
firm of Cary-Smith & Ferris, 1903-10; since then 
in independent practice, which has become very 
large, designing and. supervising construction of 
many vessels of steel of from 3,000 to 10,000 tons 
capacity, government dredging and harbor and 
transport vessels; among his clients the Atlantic, 
Gulf & West Indies S..S. Lines, Mallory, Clyde, 
Red ‘“D,’: Porto Rico, and Ward Lines, Am. 
Transportation Co., Munson Steamship Line, Mex- 
ican Navigation Co., Clinchfield Navigation Co., 
Dollar Line, Pacific S.S. Co., Old Diminion S. 
S. Co., Eastern S.S. Lines, C..D. Mallory & Co., 
Submarine Boat Corp., City of New York, Insu- 
lar Line and carried on and supervised construc- 
tion of the greatest number of vessels, in the great- 
est number of yards, and the greatest numbr of 
ships in any one yard than any person in this 
country. When the war came on was persuaded 
by General Goethals, the first head of the Shipping 
Board, to accept appointment, April, 1917, as 
Naval Architect and Consulting Engr for the 
Emergency Fleet Corpn, chosen because he was 
practically the only American architect who had 
specialized in merchant vessels, and was the best 
. American authority on standardized ships, having 
designed several for the Submarine Boat Corpn. 
This position, reluctantly accepted because it in- 
volved much sacrifice, was held until he had him- 
self completed or had approved submitted designs 
of practically all- the types of vessels that were 
built under the auspices of the U. S. Shipping Bd, 
among others three standardized types of vessels, 
of 5,000 tons, 7,500 tons and 9,000 tons capacity, 
-as well as 10,000-ton, 17-knot special troop ships, 
and a standard type of wooden ship, known as the 
Ferris type; the success of the Shipping Board 
shipbuilding programme being largely due to his 
diligence and knowledge, not only in standardiza- 
tion but also in simplification of design and co- 
ordination of industry, making possible the fabrica- 
tion of plates and parts of ships at many mills 
and factories, structural, bridge and tank shops, 
leaving to the shipyards the assembling and launch- 
ing parts of the programme. Resigned after hav- 
ing completed the constructive basis of the Emer- 
gency Fleet programme and returned to successful 
individual practice, in which continues. Mem. 
Soc. Naval Architects and Marine Engrs and 
other professional organizations,

FOHS, F. Julius, 60 Broadway, ‘New York, N. 
Y.; First National Bank Building, Tulsa, 
Okla., and Kirby Bldg., Dallas, Tex. 

Consulting Petroleum Geologist; b. New York, 

N. Y., March 1, 1884; s. Mark E. and Fredericka 

(Baum) Fohs; family moved to Marion, Ky, in 

1890; ed. in schools there, and early began special 

studies of geology and related scientific subjects; 

m. Henderson, Ky, 1905, Cora Baldauf; two dau., 

Ella, Frances. In 1901 became field asst, U. S. 

Geol. Survey, but soon resigned in order to take 

up work for a Cleveland company for which he 

made a report on mineral properties and for whom 
he was put in charge of lead, zinc and spar mines; 
apptd March, 1905, asst geologist of the Ky 

Geol. Survey. His attention was for the first few 

years directed to lead, zinc, spar, coal and other 

mineral deposits, but he became a close student. of 
oil resources and petroleum geology, and in March, 

1912 opened an office at Lexington, Ky., with the 

view to specializing in oil land investigations. As 

a_result of his careful investigations many new 
oil and gas pools have been opened and their 
limits defined, and among those recommended by 
him_in advance of development are the pools at 

El Dorado, Kansas; Elk Basin and Big Muddy, 

Wyo; Blackwell, Garber, Billings and Catfish, 

Okla.; the Gunsight pool in Texas, and opened up 

an entirely new oil field on the Mexia fault zone 

in. Northeast Texas. The only diversion from 
regular oil work in recent years was the inves- 
tigation which he and his assistants recently un- 
dertook of the mineral resources of Palestine, His 
operations are independent, although he has done 
professional work for many leading producers, 

notably with the group of companies headed A. E. 

Humphreys, Sr., of Denver, and he has been as- 

sociated as consulting geologist, director, vice- 

pres. or mem. of the Exec. Bd in the development 
of new_pools with the Merritt Oil and Gas Co. 

(later Merritt Oil Corpn), Duluth & Oklahoma 

Co. (later Milliken Co.), Humphreys Petroleum 

Co., Selby Oil and Gas Corpn, Hazelwood Oil 

Co., Sheppard Oil Corpn, O. H. Shoup and As: 

sociates, Red Bank Oil Co., Dixie Oil Co., Mid- 

Continent Petroleum Co., Homaokla Oil Co., New- 

block Oil Co., Boyd Oil Co., and others. Has 

written monographs on various mineral resources 


as well as on oil subjects, including: ‘‘Future of 
Oil Production in the United States,’ ‘‘Future 
of Oklahoma Oil Fields,’ ‘““The Geology of Texas 
Oil Fields,” ‘‘Third of Kansas-Oklahoma Oil . 
Field Remain Undeveloped,’ ‘‘Gulf Cretaceous . 
Oil Fields.’’ Mem. A.I.M.&M.E.

GOETZENBERGER

R., Thomas R. Second Lt, Engrs, June 12, 1880;

charged from Vol. service Dec. 31, 1898) ; Maj., 
U. S. Eng Corps, Feb. 7, 1900; Lt Col, Engrs, 
March 2, 1907; Col, Dec. 38,1909; Maj.-Gen., 
March 4, 1915; retired Nov. 15, 1916. Attached to 
Dept of the Columbia under Gen. N. A. Miles, 
1882-84; then transferred to Cincinnati, Ohio, as 
asst to Lt Col W. E. Merrill, who had charge of 
impvt of Ohio River for navigation, there gaining 
his first experience in the constrn of canals, locks 
and dams; instr, 1885-88; asst prof., 1888-89; 
civil and mil, eng, U, S. Mil. Acad., then returned 
to work on Ohio River at Cincinnati, Ohio, and 
Nashville, Tenn.; commd Lt Col. of Vols, at out- 
break of War with Spain, and apptd chief engr, 
1st Army Corps, May 9, 1898, serving throughout 
the war, and honorably discharged from Vol. ser- 
vice Dec. 31,.1898; detailed to Gen. Staff of the 
Army, and assigned spl duty of planning the for- 
tification about the Southern end of Rhode Island. 
During his service had large experience in canaliz- 
ing of various rivers, had supervision of the Mus- 
sel, Shoals Canal constrn on the Tenn. River; had 
constructed near Chattanooga a canal 14 miles 
long, 70 to 100 feet wide, and six feet deep, with 
eleven locks and an aqueduct, 900x60 ft.: also the 
Colbert Shoals Canal. In 1907 President Roose- 
velt found himself confronted with a problem as to 
the management of the Panama Canal project, The 
Civilian engrs, Wallace, Stevens & Shonts, who 
had been at the head of the’ work; had each re- 
signed after brief service on the field, and to pre- 
vent disruption of operations at'a critical time by 
another experiment with civil control, Pres. Roose- 
velt decided to appoint a head engr from the Army 
and placed at the head of Canal Commn Col Goe- 
thals, who had charge of the work until its com- 
pletion with success in 1914, making and securing 
the approval of the various changes in and impvt 
of original plan, including the adoption of the lock 
type of canal, the widening of the canal and locks 
and other imptvs both in eng and administration; 
first civil Governor Panama Canal Zone. Chair- 
man of Bd, apptd under Adamson 8-hour law, 
1916; State engr of New Jersey, 1917; gen. mer, 
Emergency Fleet Corpn, April-July, 1917 (re: 
signed); apptd acting Q.M. Gen., U. S. A., Dec. 
18, 1917; chief div. of Storage and Traffic, Gen- 
eral Staff, Feb., 1918, and chief of Div. af Pur- 
chase, Storage & Traffic, April, 1918; also served 
on War Industries Bd; relieved from active duty 
at own request, March, 1919. Engaged in practice 
as cons. engr; head of firm, George W. Go*thals 
& Co., New York; cons. engr, New York Port 
Authority. Received thanks of Congress by Res- 
olution March 4, 1915, for ‘Distinguished Service 
in Constructing Panama Canal”; D.S.M., 1918, for 
“especially mentorious and conspicuous service” 
im reorganizing the Quartermaster Service in War 
time; commandeur Légion d’Honneur (France) ; 
also medals from Nat. Geog. Soc., Nat. Inst. So- 
cial Sciences, Civic Forum. Mem. Am. Soc. C.E.

GOTSHALL, William Charles, 44 West 44th St., 
New York, N. Y. : 

Civil and Elec. Engr; born St. Louis, Mo., 
May 9, 1875; s. Daniel H. and Minnie (Wort- 
mann) Gotshall. Began connection with elec- 
trical work with the Missouri Electric Light & 
Power Co., then became locating engr for the St. 
Louis & Eastern Railroad; rebuilt the Cairo Elec- 
tric Railway, at Cairo, Ill. and operated it, and 
built, successively, the Belleville (Ill.) Electric 
Railway, Marshalltown (Iowa) Railway and 
Lighting Plant, Muncie Electric Railway, Muncie, 
Ind., the Grand Avenue Railway, in St. Louis; 
then, as chief engr of the Union Depot Railway 
- Co., of St. Louis, undertook the rehabilitation 
and electrification of the entire system of that 
company, involving the first introduction and util- 
ization of a 38-wire system on electric railways. 
Since that time he has devoted chief attention to 
electric railways, pioneering in improvements in 
that class of construction; converted the Second 
Avenue horse-car line in New York into a con- 
duit electric road; became president and chief 
engr of the New York and Portchester R. R. Co., 
which, built at a cost of about $20,000,000, was 
the first high-speed electric railroad line laid en- 
tirely on its own private right of way, without 
a single grade-crossing, with many pioneer fea- 
tures for speed and safety. Since then devoted 
to the purchase of railroads and their rehabilita- 
tion along the most modern and improved methods 
of construction, maintenance and electrical opera- 
tion, including, besides many in this country, 
others in Europe and Africa. Mem. Am. Soc. 
COE CALI ELE: Contbr to railway and elec. 
journals on electric railway problems; writer of 
the article on Railway Economics in the Encyclo- 
pedia Americana, and a book, Electric Railway 
Economics, 1904. Commissioned Major of Engrs 
in 1917, and remained until after the Armistice 
im_active service. Fellow, American Geog. Soc. 
(New York); mem. Adirondack League. Clubs: 
Automobile of America, New York Athletic, Rail- 
road, Lotus, Explorers, Oakland Golf (New 
York); Royal Automobile (London, England).

HAMMER (Major), William Joseph, Hotel 


Earle, 103 Waverly Place, New York, N. Y. 
Consulting Elec. Eng; b. Cressona, Schuylkill 
County, Pa., Feb. 26, 1858; s. William Alexander 
and Martha Augusta (Beck) Hammer; ed. in 
public and private schools, Newark, N. J., and 
University lectures abroad; m. Cleveland, Ohio. 
Tan. 3, 1894, Alice Maud White;, one dau., Mabel 
White Hammer. Asst to Edward Weston, of 
Weston Malleable Nickel Co., 1878-79; in Dec., 
1879, became asst to Thomas A. Edison in his 
laboratory at Menlo Park, N. J.; appt first chief 
electrician of the Edison lamp works, 1880-81; 
sent by Mr. Edison to England, 1881, to asst in 
forming his English Edison Co., of which be- 
came chief engr, 1881-82, and built in London the 
first Edison central station for incandescent elec. 
lighting in the world (of 3.000. lights), Jan. 12, 
1882. Chief engineer of German Edison Co., 
Berlin, 1883-84; returned to U. S. in fall of 1884, 
and took charge of Mr. Edison’s personal exhibit 
and those of eight other Edison interests at the 
Franklin Inst. Elec. Expn. Became an incorpor- 
ator, and secretary of Sprague Elec. R. R. and 
Motor Co.; confidential asst to Edward H. John- 
son, pres. of parent Edison Electric Light Co., 
and became chief insp. of central station. making 
elec., mech. and fin. reports upon the various sta- 
tions throughout the U. S., 1884-86; mgr and chief 
engr, Boston Edison Elec. Illuminat. Co., 1886- 
88; cons. engr to Cincinnati Expn, of 1888: went 
abroad. 1889, as personal representative of Thomas 
Edison at the Paris Internat. Expn of that 
year. Opened office in New York as consulting 
elec. engr, and has since been so engaged. Sec. 
and expert, Aeronautics Com. Hudson-Fulton 
Celebration, 1909. - Author: “Chronology of Avia- 


tion,’ “Radium and Other Radioactive Sub- 
stances,” ‘Edison and His. Inventions,’ co- 
author of ‘‘Navigating the Air’ (official book 


of the Aero Club of America), 1907; has written 
many papers, monographs, etc., on the Incan- 
descent Electric Lamp; Selenium and its Indus- 
trial Applications: High ‘Tension Railroads; The 
Poulsen Telegraphone; High Furnace Gas En- 
gines; The Steam Turbine; Lightning Phe- 
momena; American and Foreign International 
' Expositions; Aeronautics; Electrical Wonders: 
Fire Insurance Regulations; National Electric 
Code, etc.; Wireless, and Long Distance Sound 
Transmission; Automatic Telephony. Phosphor- 
escence, Fluorescence and ‘“X” Rays, Ultra 
Violet Light, etc. Was commissioned a Major, 


U. S. Army, June 4, 1918, and appointed a 
member of the Inventions Section, War Plans 
Div., and on Dec, 13, 1918, received a commis- 
sion as a Major on the General Staff, U.S.A.; was 
stationed at the War College for over a year and 
at the War Dept about six months, having charge 
of electrical and aeronautical war inventions, and 
did special work at the Patent Office and with 
the Alien Property Commission. Fellow, life 
mem. and ex-v.-p., A.I.E.E.; mem. and ex-v.-p., 
N. Y. Electrical Soc.; fellow, A.A.A.S.; charter 
mem.,, Edison Medal Assn, Assn of Edison Illu- 
minating Cos, and Pres. Edison Pioneers, 1920; 
was for two terms chmn com. on standard rules 
for elec. constrn and operation, N.E.L.A., and 
pres. Nat. com. on standard elec. rules, which 
prepared and promulgated the “National Electric 
Code;”’ was two years pres. Franklin Experimental 
Club; mem. Franklin Inst., Agassiz Natural His- 
tory Soc.; incorporator, ex-v.-p. and dir, Aero. 
Soc. of America; also is or has been mem. Inst. 
Radio Engrs, fellow Am. Physical Soc.; mem. 
Aero Club of America, Mineralogical Soc., Illu- 
minating Eng. Society, Society American Mil. 
Engrs, Military Order of the World War, and 
Engineers Club of New York. Was mem. of the 
‘Curie’? Radium Award Com. of Franklin Inst., 
and represented A.I.E.E. at the Hall of Fame 
ceremonies; chmn, Jury on Telegraphy, Telephony 
and Wireless, St. Louis Expn, 1904, and on Com. 
to Organize Internat. Elec. Congress of 1904. 
Awarded the. John Scott Legacy Medal and 
premium, 1902 (for his telephone relay and long- 
distance sound experiments) by the Franklin 
Inst., which also, 1906, awarded him the Elliott 
Cresson gold medal for his historical collection of 
incandescent electric lamps. This collection, the 
result of 384 years’ research, has been named ‘“‘The 
History of an Art,’’ and is set up in an attractive 
manner in the Engineering Societies Bldg, New 
York, covering the development of the incan- 
descent lamp from 1878 to 1913; it also was 
awarded a special silver medal at the Internat. 
Elec. Expn, at the Crystal Palace, London, 1882, 
and the “Grand Prize’ of Louisiana Purchase 
Expn, St. Louis, 1904. Republican. Reformed 
Episcopalian. :

Heisler geared locomotive, which was first built 
at the Dunkirk Eng. Co.’s plant. Following death 
of Mr. Nichols, was employed in eng dept of 
Bement, Miles & Co., on large machine tools, for 
several years. Succeeded in interesting George 
Burnham, Sr., prs., Baldwin Locomotive Works, 
in the Heisler locomotives, and a plant, controlled 
by Mr. Burnham, at Erie, Pa., was for several 
years devoted to their mfr for use in mining and 
lumbering industries in U. S. and all over world; 
later the Heisler locomotive works was capitalized 
by Erie business men and the plant, with in- 
creasing enlargements, has ever since been en- 
gaged in mfg Heisler geared locomotives. Before 
disposing of interests in locomotives, developed, 
at Erie, a high duty reciprocating pumping en- 
gine, the manufacture of which was later carried 
on at a plant erected in Ohio as the Heisler 
Pumping Engine Co., which he operated as v.-p. 
and chief engr for several years; many of these 
large size, in both vertical and horizontal types, 
were mfd and installed in a large number of the 
most prominent plants of this country. Plant 
was successfully operated until the business de- 
pression of 1907-11, which, combined with the 
introduction of competitive medium-sized turbines 
and turbine-pumping outfits, led to the discontin- 


uance of the plant; joined the mech. eng corps. 


of Am. Locomotive Co., into which the former 
Brooks and other locomotive works had bees 
merged, and there developed and invented many 
improvements in locomotives and machine tools. 
The list of Heisler inventions includes, besides the 
Heisler locomotive engine and various types of 
pumping engines and machinery, steam road rol- 
lers, water works pumping machinery, barometric 
condensers and a wet type vacuum pump; also 
two dozen or more inventions for the American 
Locomotive Co. (locomotive appliances, revers- 
ing gear, trucks, powdered fuel feeds, reverse 
levers, rotative vibratory testing machine, locomo- 
tive coal-passers, locomotive draw-bar buffer, etc.), 
as well as other important improvements in loco- 
motive engines; with Alco (fuse) Mfg Co., con- 
trolled by Am. Locomotive Co., at their Provi- 
dence plant, at beginning of the World War, and 
developed devices for mfg shells and ammunition; 
later was mech. engr of Washington Steel and 
Ordnance plant, devoted to the mfr of large ar- 
mor-piercing shells, and later to high-explosive 
shells; developed rolling mill spl shell mfg ma- 
chines and steel plant equipment. Practically all 
of his many inventions were put into practice and 
regular service. Now in charge of mech. Eng. 
dept. of Gen. Supt. office, General Electric Co. 
Mem, A.S.M.E. Club: Mohawk (Schenectady).

Battery Place, New York, N. Y., and 4

wood, Chislehurst, England. ’ 

Naval Architect, Marine Engr; b. Hartlepool, 

England, June 23, 1870; s. John and Mary Ellen 

Isherwood; ed. in schools at Hartlepool; m. Annie 

Mary Fleetham; two children. Leaving school at 

the age of fifteen, entered on apprenticeship as

various capacities to 1896; shipwright surveyor on 
staff of the principal surveyor of Lloyd’s Register 
of Shipping, and serving to 1907; while there 
made intensive study of ship constrn with an en- 
deavor to work out improvements which should 
increase the strength without sacrificing the carry- 
ing capacity of ships, and devised the theory of 
longitudinal constrn; severed his connection with 

Llioyd’s Register in order to devote himself to the 

development of his plans; during winter of 1907- 

08 his sytem was first put into operation in the 

constrn, in the yard of R. Craggs & Sons, Ltd., 

Middlesborough-on-Tees, of the “Paul Paix,” an 

oil tanker of 6,600 tons deadweight, built for Len-. 

nard’s Carrying Co., and soon after at the same 
yard the shelter-deck River Plate liner “Gascony”’ 
of 5,660 tons deadweight was built for David Mac: 

Iver Sons & Co., Liverpool. The success of these 

and other vessels, created during the next few 

years, established the Isherwood System as a suc-

cessful improvement on ship constrn, so that now

started and for five years editor of a paper called 
“Castings.”’ During all this time was in cons. 
eng. work, and finally gave up all other interests 
to devote time to impvt of existing foundries, 
design of new ones, and helping firms out of 
foundry troubles; developed large eng. organiza- 
tion, The H. M. Lane Co. (of which is pres.), 
and has served many hundreds of concerns. About 
twenty years ago started investigation into rela- 
tionship of core sands, core binders and molding 
sands to the structure of the resulting casting, 
and this led to a very extensive series-of research 
and experiments carried on in about 200 foundries; 
also has had many laboratories working on the 
problem under his direct supervision. ‘The results, 
which’ have appeared in papers published by 
various associations, are now the basis of foundry 
practice in United States and largely abroad. Ihn- 
ventor and patentee of a skew crane, spl ladle 
cranes, adjustable core racks, suspended cage 
monorail system and patents covering spl bldg 
design; also other devices not patented as well 
as his patented inventions, including the most 
extensively used core and mold ovens, in use all 
over the world (more than 900 in U. S. alone). 
During 1923 made two trips to Europe to ad- 
vise in the rearrangement of several manufacturing 
plants in England and France. Mem. British

MacDowell; descended from Charles MacDowell,

by-products of the packing industry; organized 
the Fertilizer By- Products Dept of Armour 
Company as Dept Mgr; in 1910 incorporated the 
Armour Fertilizer Works of which has been presi- 
dent and director since 1911. Also vice-pres. and 
director of Armour & Company, dir. Garfield Nat. 
Bank, N.Y., etc. Has been a dominant factor in 
the development of the by-products business of the 
packing industry, the manufacture of blood album- 
en, ete., and personally instrumental in initiating 
modern improvements in the fertilizer industry, 
such as securing better chemical control of opera- 
tions, economic handling and mixing of ingredients, 
improvements in sulphuric. acid manufacture, de- 
velopments in the fixation of atmospheric nitrogen, 
etc. Past pres. 1904-06, and 1920-22, National 
Fertilizer Assn. In 1915-16, with associates de- 
veloped and since operated the first producing pot- 
ash mine in the During the late War _ Direc- 
tor of Chemicals Div.; War Industries Bd, in 
charge of Chemicals and Explosives Raw Materials 
entering into the War programmes until dissolution 
of the Board in 1919; while thus engaged was per: 
sonally instrumental in making permanganate of 
potash, used in the early gas masks; technically 
pure carbonate of potash, which helped to solve 
the U. S. optical glass problems; the development 
of a substitute catalyst suitable for the production 
of sulphuric acid, etc. (this work done in labs. 
of Armour Fertilizer Works or at the Mellon Inst. 
of Industrial Research, Pittsburgh). Was an asso- 
ciate tech. economic advisor to the Am. Commn 
to Negotiate Peace, Am. representative. on the 
Com. on Germany, Com. on Sales of War Stocks, 
Com. on Dyestuffs, etc.; assisted in preparing 
the chemical and other sections of the Treaty 
and witnessed the signing of the Treaty; received

gium, Chevalier Legion d’Honneur (France),

sections), Internat. Chamber of Commerce; chmn.

MAIN, Charles T., 200 Devonshire St., Boston; 
res. Winchester, Mass. 

Engineer, Designer of Industrial Plants; born 
Marblehead, Mass., February 16, 1856; son 
Thomas and Cordelia (Reed) Main; ancestry 
on both sides American families established in 
Colonial days; .B.S. (department mech. eng.), 
Mass. Inst. Tech., 1876; asst in dept mech. eng. 
in same, 1876-79; m. 1883, Elizabeth F. Apple- 
ton; children: Charles R., Alice A., Theodore. 
Draftsman in Manchester (N. H.) mills, fall of 
1879 until Jan. 1, 1881, when became engr, 
Lower Pacific Mills, Lawrence, Mass.; promoted 
asst supt, March, 1886, and supt, July, 1887-92, 
having charge of operation of the Lower Pacific 
Mills. During his eleven years with that plant 
he directed its reorganization and rebuilding. In 
1892, resolving to retire from administrative work 
to devote himself more completely to eng. opera- 
tions, engaged in eng. and mill work at Provi- 
dence, R. I., 1892-93; then with F. W. Dean, 
Jan., 1893, formed firm of Dean & Main, engaged 
in textile and other industrial work until Jan., 
1907, when firm dissolved. Since then engaged 
in independent operations under his own name. 
Has designed, constructed and equipped many 
textile mills, industrial plants, steam power and 
water-power installations, etc., and hydro-elec. 
developments, one of the largest being that of the 
Montana Power Co., developing about 250,000 
h.p.; also designed and constructed the Wood 
Worsted and Aver Mills in Lawrence and many 
other large textile plants, and reorganized others. 
Served as cons. engr of many projects, also as 
expert witness in litigated cases, and as referee in 
arbitrations, and as valuator of numerous indus- 
trial plants. Served three years as alderman in 
Lawrence, Mass.; also trustee public library and 
mem. school com.; eleven years on Water and 
Sewer Bd, Winchester, Mass. Mem. A.S.M.E. 
(mgr 8 years. and pres. 1918), Am. Inst. Cons. 
Engrs, Am. Soc. C.E., Boston Soc. C.E: (past 
pres.): life mem. Corpn of Mass. Inst. Tech. 
Contributor to tech. press and to proceedings of 
professional societies. Dir. Mass. Trust Co.,

Tenn. Eastern Elec. Co., Berkshire Cotton Mfg 


Co.; trustee Winchester Savings Bank. Clubs: 
Engineers, Exchange (Boston); Engineers (New 
York); Calumet, Winchester Country (Winches- 
ter, Mass.).

1906, the proc. inv. by him for continuous produc- 
tion of calcium carbide through the heat developed 
by resistance in a molten carbide conductor. 
Wrote an article in 1875 formulating the hypoth- 
esis that all atoms of matter are compounds of 
still simpler and smaller particles of matter, and 
held that ali matter is one in the ultimate and 
that the difference in the various forms of matter 
and manifestations of force is due to the difference 
in the relative positions and motions of the ulti- 
mate atoms; this article was published long after 
written in the Sci. Am. Supplement, May 11, 
1889, but at the time it was written (at the age 
of 22) calmly disputed one of Herbert Spencer’s 
fundamental theories of force by contentions since 
largely demonstrated as true by later scientific 
discovery. Author: ‘‘Science of Poetry and 
Philosophy of Language’ (Funk & Wagnalls), 
1910. Ardent advocate of the cause of National 
Defense. His book “Defenseless America’’ (1915), 
and the motion-picture play “‘The Battle Cry of 
Peace,” were among the most widely distributed 
and most potent factors in arousing American 
patriotism to the realization of the need for pre- 
paredness. Prominent as lecturer on patriotic

Sibley Coll, Cornell Univ.; Alpha Delta Phi; 
m. Boston, Mass., Nov. 24, 1892, Sarah Boyd

Grosvenor. After leaving Lawrenceville School 
became machinist apprentice, Bement, Miles & 
Co., Philadelphia; later in drafting room, Phoenix

Cincinnati, 1897-1909; since then sec. and dir.,

ern type of radial drill, having been first to 
double the number of speeds and feeds formerly 
furnished and to supply means for obtaining 
them mechanically, reading depths from zero. 
tripping the feed at various points, lowering the 
arm at double the elevating speed, etc.; also 
originator of the first high speed lathe, and in- 
ventor of many other improvements in machine 
tools. Devised formula for ascertaining power 
required to drive drills at various speeds and 
feeds. Author: “Some Fundamentals of Thrift,” 
“Large Search Light Projectors,’ “History of the 
Drilling Machine,” “Systematic Machine Design- 
ing,” “A Simple and Effective Method of Shop 
Cost Keeping,” ‘‘Depreciation of Plant and Its 
Relation to General Expense,” “The Premium 
Plan. of Labor Remuneration,” “An Efficient 
Routing and Follow-Up System,” “An Introduc- 
tion to the Engineer,” and more than fifty other 
technical articles on eng. topics, Also published 
(1901) ‘“‘Fifty-Six Points of Vantage” and (1906) 
“Ancestry and Descendants of Lieut. Jonathan 
and Tamesin (Barker) Norris.”” Served on Coun- 
cil of Nat. Defense 1917: mech. engr Ordnance 
Dept at large. 1918. Participated actively in Lib- 
erty Loan, War Chest and Red Cross drives 
Junior 1892, mem. since 1898 A.S.M.F. (elected 
mgr for three years, Oct. 1, 1920): chmn, Cin- 
cinnati Section, 1919: one of the founders of the 
National Metal Trades Assn: charter member. 
Army Ordnance Association. Mem. New Eng- 
land Soc., Ohio Commandery. Loyal Legion;

engr for New York Steam Corp. Organized and 
became pres. The Ammonia Corp. and Niagara 
Ammonia Co.; built first plant in U. S. for fixa-

ing. Entered service as Capt. Engineers, 1917,

gas plants, Mar., 1918, appointed Chief of Pur-

appointed Asst. Chief of Chem. Warfare Service, 
A.E.F.; appointed by Commander-in-Chief, one of 
three members representing A.E.F. on Internatl 
Gas Com.; July, 1918, made a Major; Aug., 1918, 
returned to U. S. to start the manufacture of mus- 
tard gas in U. S., returning to France imme- 
diately after plant started. Jan., 1923 appointed

his well known regulating socket, which was the 
first practical device for “turning down’’ or con- 
trolling the light or candle power of incandescent 
elec. lamps without the use of wasteful resistance, 
thereby placing the incandescent lamp on a par with 
gas. Present during tests of first elec. ry. instal-

more), suggested and patented various improve- 
ments which were subsequently adopted and used 
on this-and other rys.; among them being the un- 
derground basic slotted conduit system which 
device does away with overhead conductors .and 
trolleys. Also high tension, stepdown, a.c. or 
“converter”. elec. ry system. by which the limita- 
tions and restrictions of the 500 V. trolley systems 
were for the first time successfully overcome. The 
underlying prin. of elec. generation, transmission, 
conversion and_ distribution, disclosed in these

ee 


patents made possible the various rapid transit 
elevated, subway and tunnel lines now operating 
in N. Y. and other large cities, and the electrifi-

notable being his method of electrically welding

and apparatus. Among others in gen. use are his 
basic patents on elec. elevator controllers, cover-

Elevator Co. and others on their elec. elevators,

SPRAGUE, Frank Julian, 421 Canal St., 
York, Y. 

Cons. Engr, Inventor; b. Milford, Conn., July 
25, 1857; s. David Cummings and Frances Julia 
(King) Sprague; os U. S. Naval Acad., Anna- 
polis, Md., 1878; 1st, New Orleans, La., 1885, 
Mary Keating; ‘ond, New Hartford, Conn., Oct. 
11, 1899, Harriet Chapman Jones. Officer U. S. 
N. 1878-84; mem, Jury of Award, Elec. Exhibition, 
Crystal Palace, Sydenham, near London, 1882; 
elec. experiments on ships of U. S. Navy at New- 
port Torpedo Station, and at the Brooklyn Navy 
Yard until retired from Navy, 1884, to engage in 
elec. work with Thomas A. Edison. Left Mr. 
Edison to organize, with E. H. Johnson, the 
Sprague Electric Railway & Motor Co. (of which 
was vice-president, 1884-90) ; introduced motors of 
novel design which created a sensation at the Elec. | 
Exhibition in Philadelphia, 1884, and later adopted 
by the Edison Elec. Light Co. for use by its 
licensed companies, this invention being the 
pioneer of the modern industrial electric motor; 


devoted following years to invention of the Sprague 
system of elec. railways and in May, 1887, took a 
contract for equipment of the Union Passenger 
Ry, Richmond. Va., with 80 motors for 40 cars, 
a rth teas overhead system and a central power 
plant for a 18-mile elec. ry. The success of this 
installation and its new features of speed and 
safety gave a great impetus to elec. ry constrn in 
U. S. and abroad, with installations at Florence, 
Italy, and Halle, Germany, and hundreds in this 
country; company was absorbed by the Edison 
Elec, Co. in 1890, and Mr. Sprague remained with 
that company as cons. engr, but in 1891 organized 
and became pres. of Sprague Elec. Elevator Co., 
developing the modern high-speed screw elevator, 
the automatic screw elevator, automatic house ele- 
vator and the dowuble-motor elevator, all widely 
adopted at home and abroad. Later developed 
the multiple unit system of train equipment which 
was installed by personal contract with Mr. 
Sprague on the South Side Elevated Ry in Chi- 
cago, and became the pioneer model and standard 
for many elevated and underground elec. railways. 
Was mem. of Elec. Traction Commn of the N. Y. 
Central Ry for four years in connection with the 
electrification of that road; and later planned the 
electrification of the Sierra Nevada Div. of the 
Southern Pacific Ry; vice-president and tech. dir, 
Sprague Elec. Co., 1898-1901; since then cons. 
engr for that Co.; also cons. engr for the Gen. 
Elec. Co., and Otis Elevator Co.; vice-pres. and 
cons. engr Sprague Safety Control and Signal 
Corpn; pres. Sprague Development Corpn, now 
pres., Sprague Safety Control & Signal Corpn, 
N. Y. C. Mem. A.I.E.E. (pres. 1892-93), N. Y 
Elec. Soc, (pres: 1904),\ Am: Soc, C.E., Am. 
Inst. Cons. Engrs; past pres. N. Y. Elec. Soc., 
Instn C.E. (British), Instn Elec. Engrs (Brit- 
ish), Inventors Guild (pres. 1916); asso. Soc. 
Naval Archts and Marine Engrs, Franklin Inst. 
Awarded medals at Phila. Elec Expn, Paris Expn, 
1889, grand prize for Elec. Developments La Pur- 
chase Expn at St. Louis, 1904, Ellicott Cres- 
son Medal (Franklin Inst.), 1904, Edison Gold 
Medal, 1910. Clubs: University, Engineers, Cen- 
tury, Railway, Bankers (New York).-
