TESLA, (Dr.) Nikola, 8 West Fortieth St., New 
York, “ine 

Scientist, Electrical Engr; b. Smiljan, Lika (a 
borderland’ of the then Kingdom of Austria- 
Hungary), 1857, Serbian by race, son of a priest 
of the Greek communion and his wife, Georgina 
Mandro, who was an inventor and the daughter 
of an inventor of considerable distinction; ed. in 
an elementary school in his native place, followed 
by four years in the lower Realschule at Gospic, 
Lika, and three years in the higher Realschule at 
Carlstadt in Croatia. It had been originally 
planned to train him for the clergy, but his studies 
developed a scientific trend which led him to se- 
cure his parent’s consent to attend the Polytechnic 
School at Gratz for four years, studying mathe- 
matics, physics and engineering, specializing in 
electricity followed by two years’ studies in phil- 
osophy and languages in the University of Prague, 
Bohemia, and at Budapest, Hungary. ._Hon. A. M., 
Yale, 1894; LL.D.,.»» Columbia,’ 1894; Sc.D., 
Vienna. Beginning in 1881, served for a while 
as asst engr in the Govt Telegraph Eng: Dept 
at Budapest, where he accomplished his first in- 
vention, a telephone repeater; later. went to Paris, 
becoming an elec. engr in one of the large com- 
panies developing the then new electric lighting 
industry. In 1884 came to'the United States of 
which country has since been resident and long 
a citizen; entered the Edison Works almost im- 
mediately on arrival, but seon went into inde- 
pendent praetice to develope the many new and 
in many cases basic, inventions and discoveries 
which have largely influenced the evolution of 
electrical science and elec. eng. Among the 
earliest of these was the invention of the poly- 
phase alternating current system for the trans- 
mission of electrical energy; the rotating field 
induction motor, and many other applications of 
the principle of rotating field induction. His sys- 
tem of arc lighting, 1886, invention of the Tesla 
motor and alternating current power  transmis- 
sion system, 1888; Tesla transformer 1891; meth- 
ods of wireless transmission, 1893; mechanical 
oscillators and generators of elec. oscillations, 
1895; researches and discoveries in radiation, ma- 
terial streams and emanations, 1896-98; high po- 
tential magnifying transmitter, 1897; system of 
transmission of energy by refrigeration, 1918; art 
of tel-automatics, 1898-99; discovery of stationary 
electrical waves in the earth, 1899; burning of 
atmospheric nitrogen and discovery of other elec- 
trical effects of transcending intensities, 1899-1900; 
method and apparatus for magnifying feeble ef- 
fects, 1901-02; art of individualization, 1902-08, 
and since 1903 research, experiment and develop- 
ment of his system of world-wide telegraphy and 
telephony; more recently working in the applica- 
tion of a mechanical principle discovered by him, 
to several types of machinery, such as reversible 
gas and steam turbines, hot air engines blowers, 
pumps, air compressors, transformer and_trans- 
mitters of power, etc; the principle enabling the 
production of prime movers capable of developing 
10 h. p. or more to each pound of weight. His 
earlier discoveries was elucidated in lectures de- 
livered by him before the American Inst. of Elec. 
Engrs, 1891, Royal Instn of Elec. Engrs, London, 
1892, Franklin Institute at Philadelphia, and N. E. 
L. A., St. Louis, 1893. The Edison Gold Medal 
of the A. I. E. E. was conferred upon him in 
1917. Fellow A.I.E.E., A.A.A.S., Am. Philos. 
Soc., etc.

WESTON (Dr.) Edward, Waverly Park, Newark, 
N 


Elec. Engr; b. Brynn Castle, near Oswestry, 
Shropshire, England, May 9, 1850; s. Edward and 
Margaret (Jones) Weston; removed in early life 
to Wolverhampton, Staffs., England; ed. National 
Schools, and St. Peter’s Collegiate Inst., Wolver- 
hampton; hon. LL.D. McGill Univ., 1903; Sc.D. 
Stevens Inst. Tech., 1904, and Princeton Univ., 
1910; m. New York, N. Y., Minnie Sidell; chil- 
dren: Coleman, Edward T. From boyhood de- 
voted to experiment in chemistry and electro- 
metallurgy and wanted to become a mech. engr, 
but owing to parental desires took up study of 
medicine and spent the ‘‘three years in association 
with duly qualified practitioners in regular prac- 
tice” required by English law as a qualification 
for medical practice, but gave spare hours to mech. 
and elec. investigation. Deciding not to follow 
medicine professionally, left England and came to 
New York, May 18, 1870. After a year with a 
small firm of mfg chemists, became chemist and 
electrician to Am. Nickel-plating. Co., 1871-72. 
Invented processes in connection with nickel-plat- 
ing which he failed to protect by patent and are 
now in universal use. In Dec., 1872, established 
for himself in nickel-plating business, continuing 
to 1875; studied dynamo-elec. machines and con- 
structed several; prepared in 1873 the first of the 
copper-coated carbons now in world-wide use in 
arc lighting, invented the disc armature, and in 
1875 took out his first patent, which was for an 
impvt in nickel-plating processes. Moved to New- 
ark, J., 1875, becoming partner in firm of 
Stevens, Roberts & Havell, mfg dynamo elec. ma- 
chines for electroplating, electrotyping, elec. light- 
ing, etc., which business was incorporated, 1877, 
as Weston Co., which was consolidated in 1881 
with the U. S. Elec. Light Co., of which was 
electrician, 1881-88; student of elec, light and 
power transmission problems, constructed various 
types of incandescent lamps and invented the hy- 
dro-carbon treatment which equalized and standard- 
ized the brilliancy and degree of resistance of all 
Since 1888 devoted to 
original investigation research and invention of 
measuring instruments and established the Weston - 
Elec. Instrument Co., of which was vice-pres. and 
gen. mgr 1888-1905, pres. since 1905, and has 
made himself the leader in the development and 
production of elec, measuring instruments of pre- 
cision, operating the largest manufacture of such 
instruments in the world. Second v.-p. Board of 
Trustees, Stevens Inst. Tech. -;Charter- mem. 
A.I.E.E. (pres, 1888-89), A.A.A.S., Am. Physics] 
Soc., Inventors Guild (pres.), Am. Electrochem.” 
Soc., Am. Chem. Soc., A.S.M.E., Illum. Eng. 
Soc.; fellow Am. Geog. Soc., Royal Soc. of Arts, 
Received medals and honors from various expns.
